provenance: Turn-1 request of a real gg responses-as-code run of the Carom end-to-end test case (TypeScript arm), reconstructed from the run's prompt/context_message events and reshaped to the submit_program tool-call protocol: the system prompt's Responses as Code section is the current system-code.hbs text, the two seeded example programs travel as synthesized `submit_program` calls each answered by the fixed `ok` tool result, and the request ends on the trailing contract notice — exactly the shape gg sends today, with `tools` pinned to the one `submit_program` definition and `tool_choice` forced to it by the probe's request builder. The SDK surface has moved since the capture (`files.readTextFile` no longer exists, and file-view headings now carry the file's total line count), so it is representative of a Carom turn-1 request rather than byte-identical to a current one. It comprises: the system-code.hbs system prompt, the Task prompt, two seeded example programs with their results, and the eight spec file views. Every byte of the captured content was sent to a model provider on a real Carom run; nothing is private. `source` records which gg event produced each message. By default the probe trims each file_view to 1500 characters (about 7k prompt tokens); a full-context probe sends them whole (about 17k prompt tokens).

## Responses as Code

Each turn, you take your turn by calling the `submit_program` tool. Its `program`
string is run as one TypeScript program: pass one whole, legal
TypeScript program — bare code, with no code fences around it and no
prose inside it — and it is processed exactly as written. All calls are
synchronous.

`submit_program` is the only tool in this session, and every reply must call it.
Each call is acknowledged with a tool result reading `ok`; what the program
produced arrives as separate messages after it. Text you write alongside the
call is recorded, but nothing reads code out of it: only the `program` string
runs. If one reply makes several `submit_program` calls, the programs run
sequentially, in order, every one of them.

Your program is compiled by `tsc` before it runs. A program it refuses
is not executed: you get its diagnostics and submit another program.

## Views

Views are the only way to read data out of your code and are provided on the
turn after they're opened. Print statements are not shown.

## Language Rules

Your program is compiled verbatim, as a whole TypeScript module. Each module
below is brought into scope by a named import binding that module alone, so a
name gg prints — here, in a search hit, in a documentation view — is written at a
call site with its leading `gg.` dropped.

## Ending your session

Turns continue until you end your session.

A program that fails does not end your session: the ending it called is revoked.
Fix the fault and end your session in a program that runs to completion.

Call `gg.session.finish` with a short summary of what you did once the work is
complete.

## Your modules

Your program is given these modules:

- `gg.files`: Read, write, edit and list the files of the workspace. — brought into scope with `import { files } from "gg";`
- `gg.shell`: Run shell commands in the workspace. — brought into scope with `import { shell } from "gg";`
- `gg.docs`: Find a module, function or type by searching, and take a documentation view back out of the window. — brought into scope with `import { docs } from "gg";`
- `gg.views`: Show the agent a file, a value, or an entry's documentation. — brought into scope with `import { views } from "gg";`
- `gg.context`: Manage the agent's own context window. — brought into scope with `import { context } from "gg";`
- `gg.programs`: Fetch a program that already ran, and hand a patched copy back to be run in its place. — brought into scope with `import { programs } from "gg";`
- `gg.session`: End the session, in the one shape this agent's role produces. — brought into scope with `import { session } from "gg";`

Search the documentation to find a function, by keyword or by naming modules
above. Open a documentation view of each function you intend to call, and write
the call on a later turn.

The SDK declares every function, whatever this run enabled, so a call to one this
run withheld compiles and then fails when it runs, naming the call. What you can
find in the documentation is what you can call.

## Reusing a program you already ran

Everything a program did before you fetch it and hand a patched copy back still
stands.

## Messages you receive

Every message you receive is headed by one of the following labels, on its own
line — a view's label is followed by `: ` and the name it was opened under —
followed by a `----` rule and then the content:

- `Task` — the task you are working on, or a message from a parent agent
- `Compiler error` — your last program did not compile, so none of it ran; the message is the compiler's error and nothing else. Fix it and resend the whole program
- `Runtime error` — your last program compiled and then threw, or was stopped by a sandbox limit; the message is the error and nothing else. Whatever the program did before it threw stands, so do not repeat that work
- `Notice` — a process notice from the harness (a mode change, or guidance)
- `Summary` — a summary standing in for older turns the harness compacted out of the window
- `Documentation` — documentation or a skill you asked to read, delivered on the following turn
- `File` — the contents of a file seeded into your context
- `View` — a value your program put into your window; the view's label follows the heading, as `View: changed-files`

For example, a file you opened a view of arrives as:

```
File
----
...the file's contents...
```

A program that ran is not announced: the views it opened are the result.

Task
----
Build **Carom**, a top-down paddle duel that runs entirely in the browser.

Your project root is `/work`. Build the game there.

## Your starting point

A TypeScript project is already in place at `/work`, and its `README.md`
describes it. Its dependencies are installed, so you can build and test right
away. It is wired up end to end: Vite builds it, Vitest tests it, ESLint lints it,
Prettier formats it, and `src/main.ts` already stands the engine up over the
page's canvas and runs the game.

What is missing is the game itself: `src/game.ts`. As seeded it is a stub whose
`initialize`, `update`, and `render` throw `"not implemented"`, and whose
`BACKGROUND` is a placeholder. The stub is written against the `CaromState` and
`CaromDebugApi` types the specification asks `src/game.ts` to declare, so the
project does not type-check until those declarations exist. That first `tsc`
failure on a fresh checkout is expected; declaring the types clears it.

## The Simple 2D engine

This build runs on the **Simple 2D** engine, installed as a dependency of
the project, so import it by its bare package name; there is nothing to add to
`package.json` for it and nothing to install.

The engine's own documentation is at `/work/engine`. Read all of it before you
start. It is the authoritative description of the engine's API; the specification
in `specs/` describes the game and does not restate the engine. The documentation
also carries a complete worked example of unit-testing a game built on it.

Build the game on the engine rather than beside it. The engine owns the frame
loop and the delta time it hands your update, the input actions, the audio, asset
loading, and the on-screen debug overlay. It also holds the game's state, by
value: each frame it hands `update` the current state read-only and keeps what
`update` returns as the next, so a frame builds the next state from the current
one rather than writing into it. Register what the game needs with the engine
and use what it gives back. What remains yours is the game itself: its
simulation and everything it draws.

## What to read first

The full specification is in the `specs/` directory at `/work`, already
present in your project. Read all of it before you start, and produce an
implementation that matches the specification exactly. `specs/overview.md` states
what you implement, which files stay as they are, the code quality the build is
held to, and the commands that run over the finished repository.

## The build interface

`npm ci` then `npm run build` must produce the static site, with no other manual
step, into `dist/` at the project root, with an `index.html` at the root of that
directory. Serving that directory as-is at the root of any static file server
must run the game; it is deployed to static hosting exactly that way. The scripts
that do this are already in `package.json`. Add a dependency only if you
genuinely need one, and run `npm install` afterward so the committed
`package-lock.json` matches.

## Driving the game in a browser

The project's Playwright and its headless Chromium are installed, so you can
serve the built game and drive it in a real browser, watch a rally, and check for
console errors.

When you launch the browser, use the project's own Playwright: import it from
your project (for example `import { chromium } from "playwright"`) or run the
project-local CLI with `npx playwright`. There is no global Playwright on `PATH`;
it lives in your project's `node_modules` like any other dependency. Launch
Chromium with the `--no-sandbox` argument, since this container has no Chromium
sandbox and a default launch fails.

## Commit your work

Your project root is a git repository, initialized before you started with the
starter files in its first commit. Your finished implementation is published
directly from this repository's commits, so work you leave uncommitted is not
published. When the build is complete, commit everything: run `git add -A` then
`git commit`, and confirm `git status` reports a clean working tree with nothing
uncommitted or untracked. A `.gitignore` already excludes `node_modules/`, the
build output, and coverage reports, so a clean tree means committing your source,
your tests, your `package-lock.json`, and your `README.md`.

Documentation: gg.files, gg.shell
----
11 matches for modules `gg.files`, `gg.shell`, showing 1-11.

Modules:
gg.files — Read, write, edit and list the files of the workspace.
gg.shell — Run shell commands in the workspace.

Functions:
gg.files.editFile — Replace the one exact occurrence of some text in a file with something else.
gg.files.listDir — List a directory, sorted by name; the default lists the workspace root.
gg.files.readFile — Read a file, as either a `TextFile` or an `ImageFile`.
gg.files.readTextFile — Read a text file and hand back its contents directly.
gg.files.writeFile — Write UTF-8 text to a file, creating parent directories and replacing what is there.
gg.shell.shell — Run a command with `sh -c` in the workspace and hand back its merged output.

Types:
gg.files.DirEntry — One entry `listDir` found: a bare name, and its kind.
gg.files.FileRead — What a read returned: a text file's window, or a picture's description.
gg.shell.ShellOutput — What a command reported when it finished.

Documentation: gg.docs.search
----
search(options?: { query?: string; modules?: string[]; type?: string; kind?: DocKind; offset?: number; limit?: number; }): DocSearch
  options?: { query?: string; modules?: string[]; type?: string; kind?: DocKind; offset?: number; limit?: number; } — The words to look for, the filters, and the page. Every field is optional, and omitting the object entirely asks for nothing, which is the one way this call is refused.
    query?: string — The words to look for, as one string. Several specific words beat a sentence; it may be left out only when a filter says what to look at instead.
    modules?: string[] — The modules to look in, each named either the way a program writes it (`gg.files`) or by gg's own id (`files`). Exact and case-insensitive, and several are a **union** — an entry in any one of them is a hit — so one call reads the whole of the surface this agent was given. An empty list is no module filter at all.
    type?: string — One type's own name, narrowing to that type and the functions whose signatures mention it — what can be done with a value of this shape.
    kind?: DocKind — `"module"`, `"function"` or `"type"`, to see only one of them. Any other word is refused.
    offset?: number — How many hits to skip, for reading past the first page. Defaults to none.
    limit?: number — How many hits to return: 20 by default, 100 at most, and zero is refused. Compare it against `total` to see how much of the answer this page is.

Defined in `gg.docs`, brought into scope with `import { docs } from "gg";`.

Search the modules this agent holds, everything it can call, and every type their signatures name.

Best match first, and a hit is one of three things: a **module** a program imports, a function it calls, or a type a signature names. The module is what a search wants first — nothing gg offers is in scope until the program has imported the module the function lives in.

Matching is case-insensitive substring matching over names, signatures, briefs and detailed descriptions, so `docs` finds `openDocsView`. A hit whose own name matched is ranked above one that merely mentions the word in a paragraph, and the query is split on whitespace, so several specific words work better than a sentence.

Nothing here is required, the filters compose with the query and with each other, and each filter is an exact lookup rather than another thing to rank: `modules` on its own, with no query, is those modules' whole directory, which is the first hop worth making. What is refused is asking for nothing at all — no query and no filter — because a search that found nothing and a search that was never given anything to look for are different answers.

The page comes back as a value **and** opens as a view labelled `search results`, so the results can be read next turn without being shown deliberately. That view is replaced by the next search rather than accumulating, and `gg.views.close("search results")` takes it away.

Returns: one page of hits, best first, beside the `total` that says how much of the answer it is.

Throws `ApiError` with `invalid-argument` for a search carrying neither a query nor a filter — a search that asked for nothing and a search that found nothing are different answers — for an unrecognised `kind`, which would otherwise silently widen a search believed to be narrow, and for a `limit` of zero, which is a page that could answer nothing.

Documentation: gg.docs.DocSearch
----
interface DocSearch { total: number; offset: number; hits: DocHit[]; }

Defined in `gg.docs`, brought into scope with `import { docs } from "gg";`.

One page of search results, and the total behind it.
  total: number — How many entries matched before paging, so a capped page is distinguishable from a whole one.
  offset: number — The offset this page starts at, echoed back, so paging needs nothing tracked on the side.
  hits: DocHit[] — The page itself, best first.

Documentation: gg.views.openDocsView
----
openDocsView(target: Function | string): void
  target: Function | string — What to document: a bound function itself, or the entry's name as a string — a module's name is its own path, as in `gg.files`.

Defined in `gg.views`, brought into scope with `import { views } from "gg";`.

Show the agent one module, function or type's full documentation: signature, description and types.

Only the types it names that have not already been shown this session are appended, so re-reading costs nothing twice. The argument is a bound function itself, as in `gg.views.openDocsView(gg.files.readFile)`, or the entry's name as a string.

It is a **view** rather than a return value, so the documentation arrives in the next prompt under a `Documentation` heading and is not available in the turn that asked for it. Asking in one turn and using it in the next is the shape that works. Opening an entry that is already open does nothing at all — the band only grows — and `gg.docs.close` takes the same name to put a view away, not the `close` in this module, which does not reach documentation.

Throws `ApiError` with `not-found` for an unknown or unbound name — searching the documentation is what says which names exist — and `invalid-argument` for an argument that is neither a function nor a string.

# Carom

## Overview

Carom is a top-down paddle duel for the browser. Two paddles face each other
across a dark field while a ball ricochets between them, off the top and bottom
walls, and off a pair of obstacles in the middle of the field. A player scores
when the ball passes the far edge behind their opponent's paddle.

Carom's defining mechanic is spin: the motion of a paddle at the moment it
strikes the ball curves the ball's flight afterward. The obstacles turn the open
field into a bank-shot puzzle.

Carom has its own name, look, spin mechanic, and obstacle layout, and its assets,
branding, and design are original to it.

The specification spans several files under `specs/`. Read all of them and build
the game they describe as one cohesive whole.

## The runtime

The game is built on the Simple 2D engine, which documents itself in the
`engine/` directory at the root of this repository. It owns the frame loop and
the delta time the game is given, input actions, audio cues, asset loading, the
canvas fit, and the debug overlay. Read its documentation before you start. This
specification states only what is specific to Carom.

## The project you build in

The project at the root of this repository is already wired up, and its
`README.md` describes it. It is a TypeScript project built with Vite, tested with
Vitest, linted with ESLint, and formatted with Prettier. That toolchain is fixed
and supplied.

### What you implement

`src/game.ts`, and any new modules you add beside it under `src/`.

`src/game.ts` exports `game`, a `Game<CaromState, CaromDebugApi>`: `initialize`
builds the state and the debug surface once and returns them together as
`[state, debug]`, `update` takes the current state as a read-only view
(`DeepReadonly<CaromState>`) and returns the next state, advanced against the
frame's delta time in seconds, and `render` is handed that next state, read-only
again, and draws it. The engine holds the state by value and replaces it with
what each `update` returns, so a frame builds the next state from the current
one rather than writing into it, and nothing but `update` and the debug
surface's poses advances the game. All three functions throw `"not implemented"`
as they stand. Implement them, and split the work across new files under `src/`
however suits you.

`src/game.ts` also declares and exports `CaromState` and the types it is built
from, exactly as this specification states them, and `CaromDebugApi`, the debug
and automation surface this specification fixes.

`src/game.ts` also exports `BACKGROUND`, a CSS color string: the field
background. `src/main.ts` hands it to the engine as the color the canvas is
cleared to each frame, so the letterbox bars around the field match the field
itself. The seeded stub exports a placeholder; replace it with the color your
field uses.

### What stays as it is

- `src/main.ts`, the entry point. It stands the engine up over the page's canvas,
  binds `game` to it, and runs.
- `src/constants.ts`, holding every figure this specification fixes.
- `index.html`, the page and the canvas the engine fits the field into.
- `.tcab/`, holding the vendored engine that `package.json` resolves the
  dependency from.
- `engine/`, the engine's own documentation.
- The configuration: `tsconfig.json`, `vite.config.ts`, `vitest.config.ts`,
  `eslint.config.js`, `.prettierrc.json`, `.prettierignore`, and `.gitignore`.

`package.json` takes one kind of change: a dependency you genuinely need, added
along with the updated `package-lock.json`. Its existing entries and scripts stay
as they are.

### Every figure comes from `src/constants.ts`

Every number, key binding, cue name, and piece of screen copy this specification
fixes is exported from `src/constants.ts` under the name this specification gives
it. Import it and use it. Where a spec states a value it also names the constant
that holds it, and the constant is authoritative. Anything this specification
does not name is yours to decide.

### Your own tests

Write unit tests for what you build, beside your sources as `src/**/*.test.ts`.
`npm test` runs them in process with Vitest, in Node, with coverage measured over
`src/`. A test stands the engine up over its own canvas and clock and advances the
game a counted number of frames, so it needs no browser. Cover the parts of the
game a person cannot see at a glance: the collision resolution, the paddle bounce
and spin, the serve, the scoring and match rules, and the AI.

### The checks the repository passes

Four commands run over the finished repository before it is reviewed:

| Command | Checks |
| --- | --- |
| `npx tsc --noEmit` | The code type-checks. A repository that does not compile is not reviewed. |
| `npx eslint .` | The code is lint-clean. |
| `npx prettier --check .` | The code is formatted. |
| `npx vitest run --coverage` | Your tests pass, with their count and coverage reported. |

They run on the repository as you leave it. `npm run typecheck`, `npm run lint`,
`npm run format`, and `npm test` run the same four locally.

### The build interface

`npm ci` followed by `npm run build` produces the complete static site into
`dist/` at the repository root, with an `index.html` at the root of that
directory as the entry point. That directory runs correctly when served as-is at
the root of any static file server. The scripts that do this are already in
`package.json`.

## Goal of this build

Produce a complete, polished, playable game that runs entirely in a browser.
This is a substantial front-end build: real-time rendered graphics, a physics
loop, multiple game states and menus, an AI opponent, and a local two-player
mode. Aim for a game a person would enjoy playing.

### Hard requirements

- Build on the Simple 2D engine, taking the frame loop, input handling,
  audio, and debug overlay from it.
- Render real graphics on the canvas, drawn as shapes and text rather than as an
  ASCII or text-only rendering.
- Draw everything in code. The build ships no art or audio files and fetches
  nothing at runtime.
- Run in the browser with no backend. Everything needed to play is
  self-contained, and no API key or credential is needed to build, run, or play.
- Hold the game's whole state in `CaromState`.
- Replace the starter `README.md` with one explaining what the game is, how to
  install dependencies, how to run it in development, how to produce the static
  production build, and the controls.

## Code quality

The code is written as for a long-lived codebase shared with human developers.

- Modules are split by concern, and each has one responsibility.
- Every fixed figure is named once and imported where it is used.
- Logic appears once; no two places implement the same rule.
- The tree carries no dead code, no commented-out code, and no leftover
  debugging output.
- Comments explain intent where the code cannot.
- The type-check, lint, and format checks pass.
- Unit tests cover the simulation.

## Coordinate system and presentation

All positions, sizes, and speeds in this specification are given in the field's
own logical units on a fixed play area of `FIELD_W x FIELD_H` (`1280 x 720`,
16:9). The origin `(0, 0)` is the top-left; `x` increases to the right and `y`
increases downward. The field center is `(FIELD_CX, FIELD_CY)` (`640, 360`).

- `FIELD_W x FIELD_H` is the game's logical design size. Fitting it to the
  browser window is the runtime's: the uniform scale that preserves the aspect
  ratio, the letterboxed centering, and the device pixel ratio. The complete
  field is therefore on screen at every window size, on load and at any pixel
  density.
- The letterbox bars around the field are the field's background color.
- Draw in logical units, and take the canvas element's own size from the runtime
  alone.
- Gameplay logic operates in logical units, independent of the rendered scale.

Every rate in this specification is per second and every duration is in seconds,
integrated against the delta time the runtime hands each update.

## Visual design

The field is dark. The left paddle, the right paddle, the ball, and the
obstacles are each drawn as a solid body in a bright color that stands clearly
apart from the field background. The two paddles are clearly distinguishable from
each other by color, and the obstacles are distinguishable from both paddles. The
palette, type, glow, and every other aspect of the look are yours.

- A dashed center net is drawn at `x = NET_X` (`640`). It is decoration and has
  no collision.
- During a match the two scores are drawn near the top of the field, player one's
  left of center and player two's right of center, and a label naming the mode
  is drawn somewhere on the field. The label's copy is yours.
- The moving ball has a motion trail: behind the ball, draw its path over the
  last `TRAIL_TIME` (`0.13`) seconds of travel, from the samples the state
  records. Its length is therefore proportional to the ball's speed, and it
  curves where the flight curved. How the trail is styled is yours.
- The title screen shows `TITLE_TEXT` and the `TITLE_ITEMS` menu, with the item
  at `menuIndex` drawn distinctly from the others. The pause and match-over
  screens draw their menus' items the same way. The how-to screen names the
  controls. The match-over screen shows the winner and the final score.

# Carom — Playfield, paddles, obstacles, and ball

This file defines the geometry of the field and the objects in it, including how
the ball collides with the obstacles. All positions and sizes are in the field's
logical units, and every figure below carries the name this specification gives
it.

## Playfield

- The field spans the full `FIELD_W x FIELD_H` (`1280 x 720`) area.
- The top wall (`y = 0`) and the bottom wall (`y = FIELD_H`) are solid, and the
  ball reflects off them.
- The left and right edges are goals. A ball whose `x + BALL_R < 0` scores for
  player two (right); a ball whose `x - BALL_R > FIELD_W` scores for player one
  (left).
- A dashed center net is drawn at `x = NET_X` (`640`) for decoration and has no
  collision.

## Paddles

- Each paddle is a rounded bar `PADDLE_W` wide by `PADDLE_H` tall (`16 x 110`),
  with `PADDLE_HALF` (`55`) its half-height.
- The left (player one) paddle occupies `x` in `[P1_X0, P1_X1]` (`[48, 64]`), so
  `P1_X1` is its field-facing face. The right (player two or AI) paddle occupies
  `x` in `[P2_X0, P2_X1]` (`[1216, 1232]`), so `P2_X0` is its field-facing face.
- A paddle moves only vertically. Its center `cy` is clamped to
  `[PADDLE_MIN_CY, PADDLE_MAX_CY]` (`[55, 665]`), keeping the paddle fully on the
  field.
- A human-controlled paddle moves at `PADDLE_SPEED` (`720`) units per second
  while a movement action is held and is otherwise stationary: with `up` and
  `down` each `1` while held and `0` otherwise, `axis = down - up` and
  `vy = axis * PADDLE_SPEED`.
- Every mover of a paddle (input, the AI, and the debug driver) sets `vy` and then
  integrates it the same way: `next = clamp(cy + vy * dt, PADDLE_MIN_CY,
  PADDLE_MAX_CY)`; if the clamp changed the value and `dt > 0`, then
  `vy = (next - cy) / dt`; then `cy = next`.
- A paddle's `vy` after integration is its actual vertical velocity for the
  frame, which is what the spin mechanic reads at contact. A paddle pinned against
  a bound therefore carries `vy = 0` while the action is held into the bound.

## Obstacles

Two obstacles sit in the field, fixed in place. Each is a rounded bar
`OBSTACLE_W` wide by `OBSTACLE_H` tall (`20 x 140`), placed mirror-symmetrically
through the field center `(FIELD_CX, FIELD_CY)`:

- Obstacle A is centered at `OBSTACLE_CENTERS[0]` (`490, 220`).
- Obstacle B is centered at `OBSTACLE_CENTERS[1]` (`790, 500`).

`OBSTACLES` holds the same two obstacles as axis-aligned rectangles, which is what
the collision below resolves against.

### Collision

Treat each obstacle as an axis-aligned rectangle with half-extents
`(OBSTACLE_HW, OBSTACLE_HH)` (`10, 70`), centered at its fixed center, the rounded
corners cosmetic. A ball is resolved against an obstacle by the following
rule:

1. Expand the rectangle `[x0, x1] x [y0, y1]` by `BALL_R` on every side. The ball
   overlaps the obstacle when its center is strictly inside the expanded
   rectangle.
2. Compute the four penetration depths: `left = x - (x0 - BALL_R)`,
   `right = (x1 + BALL_R) - x`, `top = y - (y0 - BALL_R)`,
   `bottom = (y1 + BALL_R) - y`. The struck face is the one with the smallest
   depth; on a tie the first of left, right, top, bottom wins.
3. Place the ball with its center `BALL_R` off the struck face: `x = x0 - BALL_R`
   for the left face, `x = x1 + BALL_R` for the right, `y = y0 - BALL_R` for the
   top, `y = y1 + BALL_R` for the bottom.
4. Reverse the velocity component normal to the struck face if it points into the
   face (`vx > 0` into the left face, `vx < 0` into the right, `vy > 0` into the
   top, `vy < 0` into the bottom); otherwise leave the velocity as it is.

An obstacle bounce leaves speed and spin unchanged, so the spin keeps curving the
ball after the bounce.

## Ball

- Every ball is a circle of radius `BALL_R` (`11`).
- Serve speed is `SERVE_SPEED` (`520`) units per second. Each paddle hit
  multiplies a ball's speed by `SPEED_MULT` (`1.04`), up to the speed cap
  `SPEED_CAP` (`980`) units per second. Wall and obstacle bounces leave speed
  unchanged.

# Carom — Balls, serving, and physics

This file defines how many balls are in play and how they are served, and how a
ball moves and interacts with the field: the physics loop, collision, and the
paddle bounce and spin mechanic. Every figure below carries the name this
specification gives it.

## The ball

One ball is in play: radius `BALL_R`, serve speed `SERVE_SPEED`, a `SPEED_MULT`
multiplier per paddle hit up to the `SPEED_CAP` cap, and the spin mechanic below.

## Physics

The runtime hands the game the real elapsed time for each frame and imposes no
timestep of its own. Every rate in this specification is integrated against that
delta time: the speeds in units per second, the spin in units per second squared,
the spin decay per second, and the hold in seconds.

The outcome of a scenario is independent of how the elapsed time was divided into
frames, beyond the drift a change in step size explains. The core is render-free:
state advances purely from the elapsed time it is handed, independent of the
canvas, of wall-clock time, and of the renderer. Any randomness runs off the
generator seeded from `state.rngState`.

### Sub-steps

On every `playing` frame the ball is advanced in `n` sub-steps of `h = dt / n`
seconds each, where `n = max(1, ceil(speed * dt / MAX_SUBSTEP))`, `speed` is
the ball's speed at the start of the frame, and `MAX_SUBSTEP` (`4`) is the most
units the ball's center travels in one sub-step.

Each sub-step does the following, in order:

1. Spin turns the velocity. With `speed = hypot(vx, vy)` and `speed > 0`, rotate
   `(vx, vy)` by `(spin / speed) * h` radians. A positive angle turns the
   direction of travel from `+x` toward `+y`, clockwise on screen. Speed is
   unchanged. A ball with `speed = 0` skips this.
2. Spin decays: `spin *= 0.5 ^ (h / SPIN_HALFLIFE)`.
3. Advance: `x += vx * h`, `y += vy * h`.
4. Resolve collisions in this order: the walls, the left paddle, the right
   paddle, obstacle A, obstacle B.

Rotating the velocity by `(spin / speed) * h` is the exact integration of a
lateral acceleration of magnitude `|spin|`, so the ball's path is an arc whose
curvature is set by `spin` and `speed`.

## Collision

The ball is a circle of radius `BALL_R`. Each paddle is the axis-aligned
rectangle `PADDLE_W` by `PADDLE_H` centered vertically on `cy`, spanning
`[P1_X0, P1_X1]` or `[P2_X0, P2_X1]` horizontally.

### Walls

The walls are resolved first in every sub-step:

- If `y - BALL_R < 0` and `vy < 0`: `y = BALL_R` and `vy = -vy`.
- Otherwise, if `y + BALL_R > FIELD_H` and `vy > 0`: `y = FIELD_H - BALL_R` and
  `vy = -vy`.

A wall bounce leaves speed and spin unchanged and plays the `wall-bounce` cue.

### Circle against an axis-aligned rectangle

A paddle is resolved by the following rule, and an obstacle by the rule the
playfield specification states for it.

1. Expand the rectangle `[x0, x1] x [y0, y1]` by `BALL_R` on every side. The ball
   overlaps the rectangle when its center is strictly inside the expanded
   rectangle.
2. Compute the four penetration depths: `left = x - (x0 - BALL_R)`,
   `right = (x1 + BALL_R) - x`, `top = y - (y0 - BALL_R)`,
   `bottom = (y1 + BALL_R) - y`. The struck face is the one with the smallest
   depth; on a tie the first of left, right, top, bottom wins.
3. Place the ball with its center `BALL_R` off the struck face.
4. Reverse the velocity component normal to the struck face if it points into the
   face; otherwise leave the velocity as it is.

### Paddles

A contact whose struck face is the paddle's left or right face is a paddle hit,
resolved by the paddle bounce below. A contact whose struck face is the paddle's
top or bottom face (an end cap) is resolved like a wall: the ball is placed
`BALL_R` off that face, `vy` is reversed if it points into the face, speed and
spin are unchanged, and the `wall-bounce` cue plays.

The ball stays inside the field and on the outside of every paddle and obstacle
at every speed up to `SPEED_CAP`.

## Paddle bounce and spin

When the ball hits a paddle:

1. Reflection angle from contact point. Let
   `offset = (ballCenterY - paddleCenterY) / PADDLE_HALF`, clamped to `[-1, 1]`.
   The outgoing angle from horizontal is `theta = offset * MAX_BOUNCE_ANGLE`
   (`55deg`). Hitting the paddle center sends the ball straight across; hitting
   the top edge sends it upward at `-MAX_BOUNCE_ANGLE` and the bottom edge
   downward at `+MAX_BOUNCE_ANGLE`.
2. Speed. `speed = min(speed * SPEED_MULT, SPEED_CAP)`, with `speed` the ball's
   speed at contact. The new velocity is `vx = dir * speed * cos(theta)` and
   `vy = speed * sin(theta)`, with `dir = +1` off the left paddle and `-1` off
   the right, so the ball travels toward the opponent.
3. Spin from paddle motion. `spin = clamp(spin + paddleVy * SPIN_FROM_PADDLE,
   -SPIN_CLAMP, SPIN_CLAMP)` (`0.85`, `+/-900`), with `paddleVy` the paddle's
   integrated `vy` for the frame. A paddle moving downward as it strikes adds
   positive spin, a paddle moving upward adds negative spin, and a stationary
   paddle leaves the spin as it was.
4. Placement. The ball's center is placed `BALL_R` beyond the paddle's front face:
   `x = P1_X1 + BALL_R` off the left paddle, `x = P2_X0 - BALL_R` off the right.

A paddle hit plays the `paddle-hit` cue. It is the only collision that changes
speed or spin.

## Spin

Spin is a signed scalar carried by the ball, `state.ball.spin`, whose magnitude
is the lateral acceleration in units per second squared. It turns the velocity
every sub-step as the physics section states, decays by half every
`SPIN_HALFLIFE` (`0.8`) seconds, and persists across wall and obstacle bounces.
Paddle hits and the decay are the only things that change it.

## Serving

At the start of the match and after each point, the ball is parked at the field
center `(FIELD_CX, FIELD_CY)` with zero velocity and zero spin, the trail is
cleared, and `state.holdTimer` is set to `HOLD_TIME` (`1.0` second). The screen
is `countdown` while the ball waits. Every `countdown` frame subtracts `dt` from
`holdTimer`; on the first frame on which the result is `<= 0`, the ball is served
on that same frame:

- `holdTimer` becomes `0`, the trail is cleared, and `screen` becomes `playing`.
- The serve travels toward `state.receiver`, the player who was just scored on.
  The first serve of a match travels toward player one (`"left"`).
- The serve leaves at `SERVE_SPEED` (`520`) at `SERVE_ANGLE` (`12deg`) from
  horizontal: `vx = dir * SERVE_SPEED * cos(SERVE_ANGLE)` with `dir = -1` toward
  `"left"` and `+1` toward `"right"`, and
  `vy = s * SERVE_SPEED * sin(SERVE_ANGLE)` with `s` either `+1` or `-1`. Whether
  `s` is fixed or drawn from the seeded generator is yours.

The ball is not advanced on the frame it is served. An elapsed `holdTimer` is the
one thing that serves the ball.

## After a point

A point is scored on the frame, after the ball has been advanced and resolved,
on which `x - BALL_R > FIELD_W` (player one scores) or `x + BALL_R < 0` (player
two scores). The scorer's score increments and the `score` cue plays. If the win
rule then holds, `winner` is set to the scorer, `screen` becomes `matchover`, and
`menuIndex` becomes `0`; the ball is left where it is. Otherwise the ball is
parked at the center, the trail is cleared, `receiver` becomes the side that was
scored on, `holdTimer` becomes `HOLD_TIME`, and `screen` becomes `countdown`.

# Carom — Menus, screens, and navigation

This file defines the game's screens, the menus, how a player moves between them,
the scoring and match flow that drives those transitions, and audio. Every figure
and every piece of screen copy below carries the name this specification gives
it.

## Scoring and match flow

- A point is scored when a ball fully passes a goal edge (`x + BALL_R < 0` or
  `x - BALL_R > FIELD_W`). The point goes to the player on the opposite side and
  increments their score.
- First to `WIN_SCORE` (`11`) points wins, and the winner leads by at least
  `WIN_LEAD` (`2`): the match is over when `p1 >= WIN_SCORE` and
  `p1 - p2 >= WIN_LEAD` (player one wins) or `p2 >= WIN_SCORE` and
  `p2 - p1 >= WIN_LEAD` (player two wins). At `10-10` play continues until one
  player is two points ahead. `state.winner` holds the winning side once a match
  is over, and is `null` until then.

## Screens

The game is a small state machine, and `state.screen` names the state it is in.
Each state has its own screen.

1. `title`, the main menu. It shows the title `TITLE_TEXT` (`CAROM`) and a
   vertical menu of `TITLE_ITEMS` (`SOLO`, `VERSUS`, `HOW TO PLAY`) in that
   order. The item at `state.menuIndex` is highlighted, drawn distinctly from the
   others. The field furniture (paddles,
   ball, obstacles, net) may show dimmed behind the menu.
2. `howto`, how to play. It names the controls and describes the spin and obstacle
   mechanics.
3. `playing`, the live game: both paddles, the ball with its trail, both
   obstacles, the net, the two scores near the top, and the mode label.
4. `countdown`, the pre-serve hold before the ball is served, rendered over the
   live field with the same furniture. It becomes `playing` when the ball is
   served.
5. `paused`, reachable from `countdown` or `playing`. It offers `PAUSE_ITEMS`
   (`RESUME`, `RESTART`, `QUIT TO MENU`) in that order, with the item at
   `state.menuIndex` drawn distinctly. The field is visible and frozen behind the
   pause menu.
6. `matchover`, shown when a player wins. It displays the winning side and the
   final score, and offers `MATCHOVER_ITEMS` (`PLAY AGAIN`, `MENU`) in that
   order, with the item at `state.menuIndex` drawn distinctly.

## What advances on each screen

`state.simTime` accumulates `dt` on every update, whatever the screen. Input is
read on every screen. Beyond that:

| Screen | What advances |
| --- | --- |
| `title`, `howto`, `matchover` | Nothing. |
| `countdown` | Both paddles (input and the AI alike), `holdTimer`, the trail. The ball sits parked. |
| `playing` | Both paddles, the ball, the trail, scoring. |
| `paused` | Nothing. Paddles, ball, and `holdTimer` are all frozen. |

Each update reads input first, then advances the screen the input left it on.

## Starting a match

`SOLO` and `VERSUS` on the title, `RESTART` on the pause menu, and `PLAY AGAIN`
on the match-over screen all start a match the same way:

- `mode` is set (`solo` or `versus` from the title; the current `mode` from the
  pause and match-over menus).
- `screen = countdown`, `resumeScreen = playing`, `menuIndex = 0`.
- Both scores are `0` and `winner` is `null`.
- `receiver = left`, `holdTimer = HOLD_TIME`, the ball is parked at the center,
  and the trail is empty.
- Both paddles have `cy = FIELD_CY` and `vy = 0`.

Returning to the title (`QUIT TO MENU`, `MENU`, leaving the how-to screen, or
`back` on the match-over screen) restores every declared field of the state to
its title-screen value, except `simTime`, `muted`, `rngState`, and `driver`,
which keep their values.

## Menu navigation

Keyboard only, through the same registered actions a match uses. Those actions,
and the keys bound to them, are held in `ACTIONS` and `BINDINGS`. Each action
below is read once per frame as a press edge.

| Screen | Action | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `title` | `p1-up` or `p2-up` | `menuIndex` moves up one, wrapping from `0` to the last item. |
| `title` | `p1-down` or `p2-down` | `menuIndex` moves down one, wrapping from the last item to `0`. |
| `title` | `confirm` | `SOLO` starts a Solo match; `VERSUS` starts a Versus match; `HOW TO PLAY` sets `screen = howto` and `menuIndex = 0`. |
| `title` | `back` | Nothing. |
| `howto` | `confirm` or `back` | Returns to the title with `menuIndex = 0`. |
| `countdown`, `playing` | `pause` | `resumeScreen` becomes the current screen, `screen = paused`, `menuIndex = 0`. |
| `paused` | `back` | Resumes: `screen = resumeScreen`. |
| `paused` | `p1-up`, `p2-up`, `p1-down`, `p2-down` | Moves `menuIndex` over `PAUSE_ITEMS`, wrapping both ways. |
| `paused` | `confirm` | `RESUME` sets `screen = resumeScreen`; `RESTART` starts a match in the current mode; `QUIT TO MENU` returns to the title. |
| `matchover` | `p1-up`, `p2-up`, `p1-down`, `p2-down` | Moves `menuIndex` over `MATCHOVER_ITEMS`, wrapping both ways. |
| `matchover` | `confirm` | `PLAY AGAIN` starts a match in the current mode; `MENU` returns to the title. |
| `matchover` | `back` | Returns to the title. |
| every screen | `mute` | Toggles the runtime's mute bit. |

`pause` is read only on `countdown` and `playing`; `back` is read only on
`title`, `howto`, `paused`, and `matchover`. When several of a menu's edges
arrive on one frame, up is applied before down, and movement before `confirm`:
a frame carrying both an up edge and a down edge moves up only, and a frame
carrying a movement edge and a `confirm` edge moves only. On `paused`, `back` is
read before the menu edges, and a frame carrying `back` resumes and does nothing
else.

## Audio

Audio plays through the runtime's cue bus. Define and play exactly the four cues
in `CUES`, under exactly these names, one per event:

| Cue | Constant | Played when |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `paddle-hit` | `CUES.paddleHit` | The ball hits a paddle's left or right face. |
| `wall-bounce` | `CUES.wallBounce` | The ball reflects off the top or bottom wall, or off a paddle's end cap. |
| `obstacle-bounce` | `CUES.obstacleBounce` | The ball bounces off an obstacle. |
| `score` | `CUES.score` | A point is scored. |

Each is a distinct short blip, so the four events are told apart by ear. Each is
played on the frame its event happens, from `update`, once per frame however
many sub-steps raised it.

Muting and the first-interaction unlock belong to the runtime. The game binds the
`mute` action to the runtime's mute bit and toggles it from any screen, then
mirrors that bit into `state.muted` every frame. The game stays fully playable
with sound muted.

## Out of scope

- Network or online multiplayer.
- Touch or gamepad input. The game is keyboard only.
- Destructible obstacles. The obstacles persist for the whole match.
- Persistence of scores or settings between sessions.

# Carom — Single player (Solo)

Solo is one of the two ways to play Carom, reached from `SOLO` on the main menu.
It pits player one, the left paddle controlled by the human, against the AI on the
right. Solo and Versus differ in who controls the right paddle: the AI here, a
second human there.

Every figure below carries the name this specification gives it.

## Controls

Keyboard only. The controls are registered actions on the `LAYOUT`
(`dual-vertical`) touch layout. Register exactly the eight names in `ACTIONS`, in
that order, each bound to the keys `BINDINGS` gives it:

| Action | Keys | Does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `p1-up` | `KeyW` | Moves the human's (left) paddle up. |
| `p1-down` | `KeyS` | Moves the human's (left) paddle down. |
| `p2-up` | `ArrowUp` | Also moves it up: Solo has one human player. |
| `p2-down` | `ArrowDown` | Also moves it down: Solo has one human player. |
| `confirm` | `Enter`, `Space` | Accepts the selected menu item. |
| `back` | `Escape` | Goes back a screen. |
| `pause` | `KeyP`, `Escape` | Pauses at any time. |
| `mute` | `KeyM` | Toggles mute. |

- `W`/`S` and `Up`/`Down` therefore both move the human's paddle, which moves at
  `PADDLE_SPEED` while a movement action is held and is otherwise stationary.
- `back` and `pause` share the `Escape` key. Read `pause` while a match is live
  and `back` on the menus, so `Escape` pauses in a match and goes back on a menu.

The AI drives the right paddle in Solo.

## HUD

During a match the two scores are drawn near the top of the field, player one's
left of center and player two's right of center, and a label naming Solo is drawn
on the field. The label's copy, and the placement and type of all three, are
yours.

## Input

- With `up` being `1` while `p1-up` or `p2-up` is held and `0` otherwise, and
  `down` being `1` while `p1-down` or `p2-down` is held and `0` otherwise, the
  human's paddle takes `vy = (down - up) * PADDLE_SPEED` and is then integrated
  and clamped as the playfield specification states.
- Both paddles move on every `countdown` and `playing` frame, the human's from
  input and the right paddle from the AI.

## AI opponent

The AI controls the right paddle in Solo. It holds no state of its own: each
frame it computes its velocity from the state below and integrates the paddle
exactly as a human-controlled paddle is integrated.

| Name | Value | Role |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `AI_SPEED` | `560` | Top speed, in units per second. |
| `AI_REACT` | `0.12` | Reaction lag, in seconds. |
| `AI_DEADZONE` | `10` | Stop distance while defending, in units. |
| `AI_HOME_Y` | `360` | Rest position, the vertical center. |
| `AI_HOME_DEADZONE` | `18` | Stop distance while returning home, in units. |

1. `target = AI_HOME_Y` and `deadzone = AI_HOME_DEADZONE`. If `screen` is
   `playing` and the ball has `vx > 0`, then
   `target = ball.y - ball.vy * AI_REACT` and `deadzone = AI_DEADZONE`.
2. `diff = target - cy`. If `|diff| <= deadzone` then `vy = 0`; otherwise
   `vy = sign(diff) * min(AI_SPEED, |diff| / dt)`.
3. Integrate and clamp the paddle as the playfield specification states.

`AI_SPEED` is below the human's `PADDLE_SPEED` (`720`), and the target is the
ball's present position offset by its present velocity rather than where a
curving or banking flight will arrive.

# Carom — Game state

`src/game.ts` declares and exports the state the game is written against. This
section is that declaration: write it into `src/game.ts` exactly as it stands
here. The state is a value the engine holds and every frame replaces, so every
field and every array is declared `readonly`: a frame builds the next state
from the current one rather than writing into it, and every reader is handed
the state as `DeepReadonly<CaromState>` in any case.

```ts
export type Screen =
  "title" | "howto" | "countdown" | "playing" | "paused" | "matchover";

export type Mode = "solo" | "versus";

export type Side = "left" | "right";

export interface PaddleState {
  readonly cy: number;
  readonly vy: number;
}

export interface BallState {
  readonly x: number;
  readonly y: number;
  readonly vx: number;
  readonly vy: number;
  readonly spin: number;
}

export interface TrailSample {
  readonly x: number;
  readonly y: number;
  readonly t: number;
}

export interface DriverState {
  readonly paddles: boolean;
  readonly ai: boolean;
  readonly vy: { readonly left: number; readonly right: number };
}

export interface CaromState {
  readonly screen: Screen;
  readonly mode: Mode;
  readonly menuIndex: number;
  readonly resumeScreen: Screen;

  readonly score: { readonly p1: number; readonly p2: number };
  readonly winner: Side | null;

  readonly receiver: Side;
  readonly holdTimer: number;

  readonly paddles: { readonly left: PaddleState; readonly right: PaddleState };
  readonly ball: BallState;
  readonly trail: readonly TrailSample[];

  readonly simTime: number;
  readonly muted: boolean;
  readonly rngState: number;

  readonly driver: DriverState;
}
```

## The type aliases

`Screen` is the top-level state machine. `countdown` and `playing` both render
the live field, and the rest are menu or overlay screens. `Mode` is the way a
match is played. `Side` names a side of the field, and player one is the left.

## `PaddleState`

One paddle. Its `x` is fixed by the side it is on, so only the vertical axis is
state.

- `cy` — center y, in logical units, clamped to
  `[PADDLE_MIN_CY, PADDLE_MAX_CY]`.
- `vy` — the paddle's integrated vertical velocity for the frame, in units per
  second: the velocity after the clamp to `[PADDLE_MIN_CY, PADDLE_MAX_CY]` has
  been applied. This is what the spin mechanic reads at contact, so a paddle
  pinned against a bound holds `0` while a movement action is held into the
  bound.

## `BallState`

- `x`, `y` — the ball's center, in logical units.
- `vx`, `vy` — the ball's velocity, in units per second.
- `spin` — the signed spin scalar, with a magnitude in units per second
  squared. Positive spin turns the direction of travel clockwise on screen and
  negative spin counterclockwise; it decays by half every `SPIN_HALFLIFE`
  seconds and changes otherwise only on a paddle hit.

Speed is `hypot(vx, vy)`, derived rather than stored.

## `TrailSample`

One recorded ball position, used to draw the motion trail: `x` and `y` in
logical units, and `t`, the simulation time in seconds at which the sample was
recorded.

## `DriverState`

Who is driving the paddles. It is inert during normal play, with `paddles`
`false`, the registered actions moving the human paddles and, in Solo, the AI
moving the right one.

- `paddles` — `true` once a control operation on the debug surface has taken the
  paddles from the player. Both paddles then follow `vy`, and the input actions
  and the AI leave them alone until a `reset`. That is what lets a scenario be
  posed and replayed exactly.
- `ai` — Solo only. While `paddles` and `ai` are both `true`, the real AI
  opponent plays the right paddle against the posed ball while the left paddle
  stays on its held velocity.
- `vy` — the vertical velocity each paddle holds while `paddles` is `true`, in
  units per second.

## `CaromState`

The whole of Carom's state. Every field is present from the moment `initialize`
returns, and every one is plain data: numbers, strings, booleans, and containers
of them, so a scenario is posed by building a state that differs in the fields
posed and read back by reading them.

- `screen` — the screen currently shown.
- `mode` — the mode the current or most recent match is played in.
- `menuIndex` — the highlighted item on whichever menu `screen` is showing.
- `resumeScreen` — the screen the pause menu resumes to, `countdown` or
  `playing`.
- `score` — the two scores. First to `WIN_SCORE`, winning by at least
  `WIN_LEAD`.
- `winner` — the winning side once the match is over, and `null` until then.
- `receiver` — the side the next serve travels toward, which is the player who
  was just scored on. The first serve of a match travels toward player one.
- `holdTimer` — seconds remaining of the pre-serve hold. It is `HOLD_TIME` at
  the start of a match and after each point, counts down to `0`, at which point
  the ball is served, and sits at `0` during a live rally.
- `paddles` — the two paddles.
- `ball` — the single ball in play.
- `trail` — the ball's trail samples, oldest first. On every `countdown` or
  `playing` frame, after the ball has been advanced, the ball's `(x, y)` and
  `simTime` are appended as a sample and every sample older than `TRAIL_TIME`
  is dropped. Parking the ball clears the trail.
- `simTime` — accumulated simulation time, in seconds. Every `update` adds its
  `dt`, whatever the screen, the paused screen and the menus included.
- `muted` — the game's readable copy of the engine's mute bit, which every
  `update` carries into the state it returns. The engine owns muting, and this
  field is what the debug surface reports.
- `rngState` — the state of the game's seeded random generator. A `reset` with a
  seed sets it, so reseeding and replaying the same calls reproduces the same
  result. A build that uses no randomness never reads it.
- `driver` — the debug driver's hold on the paddles.

## The contract

The declaration above is what the debug surface reads and poses.

- Keep every field under its declared name, type, and meaning.
- `initialize` builds the whole state in one go, so every field is present by
  the time a frame can observe it, and none of them is optional.
- Fields you add hold derived data you can rebuild from the declared ones. A
  `reset` restores the declared fields to their title-screen values, so those
  fields are the whole of the authoritative state.
- The state handed to `update` is the whole of the game, and the state `update`
  returns is the whole of the next frame. Every value the game carries from one
  frame to the next lives in it; nothing is kept in a module-level variable or a
  closure.
- The state is handed over read-only, as `DeepReadonly<CaromState>`, to
  `update`, to `render`, to every diagnostic source, and to every operation of
  the debug surface. `update` and the surface's poses return a new `CaromState`
  built from the one they received; `render`, the sources, and `snapshot`
  return no state. The type is what guarantees that rendering changes nothing
  and that nothing but a transition advances the game.

# Carom — Debug and automation surface

Carom carries a small debugging and automation surface so the game can be driven
and inspected from code without touching the keyboard or waiting on real time.

You implement it. Every operation this file specifies is a deliverable, and the
build's `initialize` returns the finished surface beside the state it built, as
the pair `[state, debug]`. The engine returns that same value from
`engine.debug`, and it is reached that way alone: nothing is installed on the
page. Every scenario driven from code reaches the game through it, so it is
present and exactly as specified here.

Each operation is a reading or a pose of `CaromState`, written in the shape of
`update`, because the engine holds the state by value and nothing holds a
writable one. A pose takes the current state, as `DeepReadonly<CaromState>`,
and returns the next `CaromState`; a reading takes the state the same way and
returns what it read. A caller drives a pose through the engine's `apply`, as
`engine.apply((s) => debug.serve(s))`, and a reading against the engine's
current state, as `debug.snapshot(engine.state)`. A pose arranges the world, and
the game's own `update` runs the real collision, the real serve, and the real AI
from there on the next frame, so a scenario driven from code behaves exactly like
one played by hand. Where the surface's implementation lives under `src/` is
yours to decide; `src/game.ts` declares and exports its type, `CaromDebugApi`.

The surface is inert during normal play, doing nothing until something calls it.

## A deterministic core

The surface rests on the simulation being deterministic: every rate integrated
against the delta time the game is given, so an interval of game time reaches the
same state however it was divided into frames. Two more properties make it
driveable from code:

- Render-free core. Game state advances from the elapsed time the game is handed,
  independent of a canvas, of the frame loop that measured it, and of wall-clock
  time. The dependency runs one way: the simulation reads nothing from the
  renderer.
- Seeded randomness. Any randomness the game uses runs off a generator seeded from
  `state.rngState`, and it keeps its whole generator state in that field, so
  reseeding and replaying the same calls reproduces the same result exactly. A
  build that uses no randomness simply never reads it.

Given the same seed and the same sequence of calls and elapsed game time, the game
reaches the same state every time.

## What the runtime provides instead

The clock, the keyboard, and the overlay belong to the Simple 2D engine,
which documents them in the `engine/` directory, and the surface carries no
operation for any of them. The engine advances the game frame by frame and can
take it off real time, it drives the actions the game registers, and it draws and
toggles the debug overlay.

What the overlay shows is Carom's, under Diagnostics below.

## The driver

`state.driver` is how the surface takes the paddles from the player, and honoring
it is the one behavior the whole surface depends on.

- While `driver.paddles` is `false`, the game plays normally: the registered
  actions move the human paddles and, in Solo, the AI moves the right one.
- Every operation that poses the game sets `driver.paddles` to `true`. From then
  on both paddles move at the held velocities `driver.vy.left` and
  `driver.vy.right`, in units per second, integrated against the frame's delta
  time and clamped to `[PADDLE_MIN_CY, PADDLE_MAX_CY]` exactly as a played paddle
  is. The input actions and the AI leave the paddles alone while it is `true`.
- `snapshot` and `reset` leave the driver as they found it.
- The exception is `driver.ai`. In Solo, while `driver.paddles` and `driver.ai`
  are both `true`, the right paddle is driven by the real AI opponent while the
  left paddle stays on its held velocity.
- `reset` sets `driver.paddles` and `driver.ai` back to `false` and both held
  velocities to `0`, handing the paddles back.

A paddle's `vy` field reports its actual vertical velocity for the frame, whoever
moved it, because that is what the spin mechanic reads at contact. A paddle pinned
against a bound therefore reports `0` while a movement action is held or a driver
velocity is set.

## The operations

The surface carries `version` (`CAROM_DEBUG_VERSION`, `1`), a plain number, and
the operations below. Values are plain numbers, strings, and booleans;
coordinates and velocities are in the field's logical units.

Each operation's first parameter is the current state, `DeepReadonly<CaromState>`.
A pose returns the next `CaromState`, built from the one it was handed, which it
leaves as it was; a reading returns what it read. The headings below name the
parameters that follow the state.

### `reset(state, options)`

Restores every declared field of the game's state to its title-screen value: the title
screen with `menuIndex` at `0`, both scores `0`, no winner, `receiver` back to
`"left"`, `holdTimer` at `0`, both paddles centered at `FIELD_CY`, the ball parked
motionless and spinless at `(FIELD_CX, FIELD_CY)`, an empty trail, `simTime` at
`0`, and the driver cleared. `options.seed` seeds `rngState`, defaulting to
`DEFAULT_SEED` (`1`).

`muted` is deliberately untouched: muting is a player preference the runtime owns.

Because it restores exactly the declared fields, any state of your own that a
frame depends on is derivable from them.

### `snapshot(state)`

A pure reading of `state`, returned as the plain object under Snapshot shape
below. It returns no state, because it poses nothing.

### `startMatch(state, mode)`

Poses the opening of a real match, with `mode` being `"solo"` or `"versus"`,
exactly as choosing it from the menu would: `screen` becomes `"countdown"`,
`holdTimer` becomes `HOLD_TIME`, both scores `0`, `winner` `null`, `receiver`
`"left"`, both paddles centered, and the ball parked. It leaves `simTime` as it
is.

The game runs from there: the countdown ticks down against the delta time and the
serve happens through the game's own code.

### `serve(state)`

Ends the pre-serve hold immediately instead of waiting it out, by setting
`holdTimer` to `0`. From a live rally it re-parks the ball, clears the trail, and
returns `screen` to `"countdown"` first, so a re-serve and a first serve behave
identically. It applies on the `"countdown"` and `"playing"` screens alone.

The launch itself is yours: on the next frame the game advances, an elapsed
`holdTimer` launches the ball at `SERVE_SPEED` toward `state.receiver`.

### `setScore(state, p1, p2)`

Sets the two scores directly, as a precondition. The win and deuce rules still
resolve through real play, so a match ends when a real point is driven.

### `setPaddle(state, side, patch)`

Poses or moves a paddle. `side` is `"left"` or `"right"`; `patch` may set `cy`
(center y) and `vy` (vertical velocity in units per second). A `vy` set here is
written to both the paddle and `driver.vy[side]`, so it persists across frames and
the paddle is still moving when it strikes the ball, which is what drives the spin
mechanic.

### `setBall(state, index, patch)`

Places and aims a ball. `index` is `0`, selecting the single ball in play. `patch`
may set any of `x`, `y`, `vx`, `vy`, and `spin`.

### `setAiControl(state, enabled)`

Sets `driver.ai`, handing the right paddle back to the computer opponent for the
rest of the driven scenario, so advancing the game runs the real AI against the
posed ball while the left paddle and the ball stay on their posed values. It
applies in Solo; `false` is the default, and `reset` clears it.

A typical scenario applies `startMatch` through
`engine.apply((s) => debug.startMatch(s, "versus"))`, then `setPaddle` and
`setBall` the same way to arrange the exact contact wanted, advances the engine a
handful of frames to run the real collision, and reads the result from
`debug.snapshot(engine.state)`.

## Snapshot shape

`snapshot` returns:

```js
{
  version: 1,
  screen: "title" | "howto" | "countdown" | "playing" | "paused" | "matchover",
  mode: "solo" | "versus",
  score: { p1: <number>, p2: <number> },
  winner: "left" | "right" | null,   // the winning side once the match is over
  muted: <boolean>,                  // whether the mute toggle is currently on
  paddles: {
    left:  { cy: <number>, vy: <number> },
    right: { cy: <number>, vy: <number> },
  },

  // The single ball in play.
  ball: { x: <number>, y: <number>, vx: <number>, vy: <number>,
          speed: <number>, spin: <number>, held: <boolean> },

  simTime: <number>,   // accumulated simulation time, in seconds
}
```

Every field is read straight off the game's state, so what the snapshot reports is
what the game holds. Two are derived rather than stored: `speed` is
`hypot(vx, vy)`, and `held` is true while a ball's pre-serve countdown is still
running, which stays true through a pause.

The game refreshes the following every frame:

- `muted` mirrors the runtime's mute bit. Refresh it from the runtime in every
  update, since the runtime owns muting and this is the game's readable copy of
  it.
- `simTime` accumulates the delta time of every update, whatever the screen.
- `holdTimer` counts down from `HOLD_TIME` to `0` and sits at `0` during a live
  rally.

## Diagnostics

The runtime's debug overlay shows the values the game registers with it as
diagnostic sources. Register at least the current `screen` and `mode`, both
scores, each ball's position, velocity, speed, and spin, and each paddle's center
and velocity, the same facts `snapshot` reports. Keep each one short enough to
read on a line, and keep every source a pure read, so watching the overlay leaves
the simulation as it is.

Registering those values is the whole of Carom's part, through
`InitApi.diagnostics`. Each source is called with the state current at the read,
as `DeepReadonly<CaromState>`, and reads off that argument: a source that closed
over the state `initialize` built would report the title screen forever, because
every frame leaves a new value behind. Drawing the panel, toggling it, and
keeping it read-only are the engine's.

Reminder: take your turn with one `submit_program` call whose `program` string is one whole, bare TypeScript program — no code fences, no prose inside it. It is processed exactly as written; text outside the call is not.
